proposedDescription: Bean common mosaic virus infects beans and several other legumes. Affected leaves may show an uneven light-and-dark green pattern, puckering or curling, and plants infected early can remain small. The virus travels in infected seed and can be carried between plants by aphids during short feeding visits. Symptoms vary with the plant variety and virus strain, and some infections are easily confused with other bean viruses. Starting with tested seed is therefore more reliable than judging seed health by its appearance.
identification: Mottled, puckered or curled bean leaves; laboratory testing distinguishes BCMV from similar viruses.
actions: Use virus-tested certified seed and resistant varieties suited to local disease risks.

proposedDescription: Bd chytrid fungus is a microscopic fungus that infects amphibian skin. It releases swimming spores into water, allowing infection to pass through wet environments. Some amphibians carry it without obvious illness, while others develop chytridiomycosis, with abnormal skin shedding, weakness or loss of normal movement. Severe outbreaks have contributed to amphibian declines around the world. A skin swab can reveal infection, but visible illness is not specific enough to identify the fungus, and detecting it does not always mean the animal has developed disease.
identification: No reliable naked-eye identification; unusual shedding or weakness warrants expert assessment and laboratory testing.
actions: Do not move amphibians between habitats; clean and disinfect field gear using wildlife-agency guidance.

proposedDescription: Beach sheoak is a tall flowering tree whose fine, drooping branchlets can make it look like a pine. Its true leaves are tiny scales arranged in rings around those jointed branchlets, and the fruits form small woody, cone-like clusters. Native across parts of Asia and the western Pacific, it has been planted widely in tropical regions. In Florida, it is one of several introduced Casuarina species that have spread into native plant communities. Counting the leaf scales helps distinguish it from related sheoaks.
identification: Drooping jointed branchlets with usually six to eight tiny leaf teeth per ring; small woody fruit clusters and scaly bark.
actions: Confirm the species before removal; avoid planting it where locally invasive and obtain professional help for large trees.

proposedDescription: Beaked hawksbeard is a leafy herb with yellow, dandelion-like flower heads and toothed or lobed leaves. The outer rays can be reddish underneath, a useful detail when similar yellow-flowered plants grow together. Mature seeds narrow into a slender beak before the tuft of hairs used for wind dispersal. Native to parts of Europe, the Mediterranean and nearby Atlantic islands, it has been introduced elsewhere. North American records include disturbed places, meadows and fields, although its local abundance varies considerably.
identification: Yellow heads with reddish undersides to the rays; toothed or lobed leaves and distinctly beaked mature seeds.
actions: Confirm with mature flowers and seeds; remove unwanted plants before seed dispersal where practical.

proposedDescription: Bean aphids are small, dark sap-feeding insects that gather on tender growth, leaves and stems. Adults are usually dull dark green to purplish black with lighter legs; both winged and wingless forms occur. Dense colonies can curl foliage and weaken young bean plants, while their sugary honeydew leaves surfaces sticky and encourages sooty mold. They can also carry plant viruses. Lady beetles, lacewings and tiny parasitic wasps often reduce colonies naturally, so the presence of aphids does not always mean treatment is needed.
identification: Dull dark aphids with pale legs and two short tailpipe-like projections; compare with the shinier cowpea aphid.
actions: Inspect young growth and natural enemies; avoid broad treatments that disrupt predators when plants are tolerating colonies.

proposedDescription: Bean flower thrips is a small insect most often found inside legume flowers. Adults are dark brown, with pale areas on the narrow wings, while males can be smaller and lighter. Feeding and egg laying can damage flowers and developing pods, reducing crop quality. The species is associated with tropical Asia and has more recently been recorded in Florida. Several thrips can share the same bean crop, so an insect in a damaged blossom needs microscopic examination before it can be confidently named.
identification: Dark brown winged thrips with pale wing areas; inspect flowers, but use a specialist for species confirmation.
actions: Check blossoms and young pods for insects and fresh injury; consult local crop advisers before selecting management.

proposedDescription: Bean root aphids are small, pale insects that feed on the roots of beans and many other plants. The wingless root-feeding forms are yellowish white with a dusting of wax and a light brown head and legs. Their life cycle can also involve Pistacia trees, where colonies develop inside swellings formed from leaf tissue. In places without those tree hosts, populations may remain on roots. This broad choice of hosts means the name describes only part of the aphid's way of life.
identification: Check roots for pale, wax-dusted aphids about 2 millimeters long; specialist examination is needed to distinguish other root aphids.
actions: Have suspected root aphids identified with the host plant recorded. Keep infested root material contained while obtaining local plant-health advice.

proposedDescription: Bean weevil is a small seed beetle that develops inside dry beans. Adults have mottled brown, black and gray wing covers and lack the long snout associated with true weevils. The larvae chew within seeds, often remaining hidden until an adult leaves a neat round exit hole. Infestations can begin in the field and continue through repeated generations in warm storage. Moving infested seed has carried the beetle widely, and apparently intact beans can already contain developing larvae.
identification: Small mottled beetles without a long snout; round holes in stored beans and pale larvae within seeds.
actions: Inspect stored beans, isolate affected lots and keep clean seed in sealed containers; seek storage-pest advice for valued planting seed.

proposedDescription: Bear’s breeches is a clump-forming perennial with large, glossy leaves cut into deep lobes. Tall flower spikes rise above the foliage, carrying white flowers surrounded by purple-toned, spiny structures. The leaf shape is familiar from classical architectural decoration. Native around parts of the Mediterranean, it is grown widely as an ornamental in sun or partial shade. Underground stems allow an established clump to spread, and pieces left in the soil can make it difficult to remove completely.
identification: Large glossy, deeply lobed basal leaves and tall spikes of white flowers with purple, spiny bracts.
actions: Place cultivated plants where their spread can be contained; remove unwanted root pieces and check for regrowth.

proposedDescription: Beardless rabbitsfoot grass is a moisture-loving grass that forms loose tufts and can spread through creeping stems that root where they touch the ground. Its narrow, flat leaves rise beneath dense, branched flower heads, usually green and sometimes tinged purple. Unlike the conspicuously bristly heads of some related grasses, its tiny flower clusters lack long awns. It grows beside ditches and waterways and on other damp ground, with a native range spanning parts of southern Europe, Africa and Asia.
identification: Look for creeping, rooting stems and compact, lobed green flower heads without long projecting bristles; a grass key is needed for similar species.

proposedDescription: Bed bugs are small, blood-feeding insects that hide in narrow spaces close to where people rest. Unfed adults are flat, oval and brown, roughly the size of an apple seed; after feeding they become fuller and redder. Young bugs are smaller and much paler. They shelter in mattress seams, bed frames, furniture and other cracks, and can travel with luggage or belongings. Finding the insect itself, shed skins or dark spotting is more useful for identification than a pattern of skin bites.
identification: Adults are flat, brown and oval; young stages are pale. Inspect seams and crevices for bugs, shed skins and dark marks, and have suspected specimens identified.
actions: Keep suspected items contained rather than moving them between rooms. Seek identification and an integrated treatment plan from a qualified pest professional.
researchNotes: EPA morphology and University of Minnesota household entomology guidance are separate institutional accounts. Bite appearance does not establish a bed bug diagnosis; no disease-transmission or medical-treatment claim is needed.

proposedDescription: Beech aphids are tiny sap-feeding insects most easily noticed through the white, woolly wax that gathers beneath beech leaves. The insects underneath are pale yellow, and their feeding can curl leaves downward. Sticky honeydew may fall onto lower foliage and support dark sooty mold. On European beech, eggs spend winter in bark crevices before colonies develop on new leaves. Infestations can spoil the appearance of leaves, although established, healthy trees often tolerate them without lasting harm.
identification: Check leaf undersides for pale aphids wrapped in white wax, sticky deposits and downward-curled leaf edges. Wool on bark alone points to other possible insects.
actions: Monitor tree condition and encourage natural enemies. Healthy established beeches often need no intervention; obtain an identification before treating persistent damage.
researchNotes: RHS practical account is independent of Kot and Kmiec's 2012 field study on Fagus sylvatica and cultivars. Do not confuse Phyllaphis fagi with the American beech blight aphid or beech scale.

proposedDescription: Neonectria coccinea is a fungus associated with bark disease in European beech. It can live in beech tissues without obvious symptoms, but it has also been recovered from declining trees and shown experimentally to cause substantial bark lesions. These injured patches can be part of more complicated tree decline involving stress and other fungi. The species is closely related to fungi involved in North American beech bark disease, so an affected tree's appearance alone cannot establish which fungus is present.
identification: Bark lesions or dieback warrant examination, but symptoms are not species-specific. Reliable identification requires laboratory work, including microscopic or DNA comparisons.
actions: Have unexplained beech bark damage assessed by a tree-health specialist. Record the host and location, and avoid assigning a fungal name from symptoms alone.
researchNotes: Important catalog distinction: modern N. coccinea is separated from North American N. faginata, historically called N. coccinea var. faginata. Castlebury et al. 2006 studied taxonomy; Langer and Busskamp 2021 independently tested European isolates. No US occurrence or introduced status inferred.

proposedDescription: Neonectria faginata is one of the fungi involved in beech bark disease in North America. The disease develops through an interaction between beech scale insects and fungi: scale feeding damages the bark, creating entry points for infection. Affected American beeches develop sunken or swollen areas of dead bark that may merge into larger cankers. The white, woolly material often seen earlier on the trunk belongs to the scale insects. Fungal identification requires closer examination than the tree's outward symptoms.
identification: Look for beech scale's white wax followed by patches of damaged, cankered bark. A plant laboratory must distinguish N. faginata from other canker fungi.
actions: Ask a tree-health professional to assess affected trees and any structural risk. Photograph bark symptoms and retain the location and host identity for diagnosis.
researchNotes: Retain separate catalog ID from N. coccinea. Castlebury et al. 2006 elevated the former N. coccinea var. faginata. NRCan's heading correctly uses N. faginata but its body retains obsolete Nectria coccinea terminology; used for the Canadian disease complex, reconciled against the original taxonomy. Do not equate the fungus with the entire disease or declare it introduced.

proposedDescription: Beech leaf disease is associated with a microscopic leaf nematode, Litylenchus crenatae subsp. mccannii. A distinctive early sign is dark banding between the veins of beech leaves, especially when viewed against the light. More affected leaves may become thick, curled or misshapen, while damaged buds produce fewer leaves and the crown gradually thins. The nematodes spend winter in buds and affect developing foliage. American, European and Oriental beeches can develop the disease, so host species alone does not rule it out.
identification: Hold a leaf toward the light to check for dark interveinal bands, and compare nearby leaves for thickening and distortion. Confirmation needs specialist assessment.
actions: Photograph several leaves and the whole tree, and contact local Extension or a plant diagnostic laboratory. Avoid transporting affected beech material to new sites.
researchNotes: Duplicate taxon context: this disease-oriented ID and litylenchus-crenatae-ssp-mccannii refer to the same named nematode subspecies; preserve both IDs pending editorial taxonomy review. Carta et al. 2020 original description and inoculation study is the underlying cause evidence; UMD supplies independent regional observations and practical recognition, while citing that research for causality.

proposedDescription: The beech tree nematode is a microscopic roundworm associated with beech leaf disease. It lives in developing buds and leaves, where its presence is linked to dark bands between leaf veins and to thickened, distorted foliage. Heavy damage can prevent buds from opening normally and leave the crown sparse. Researchers distinguished this North American subspecies from the previously described Japanese Litylenchus crenatae using body features and DNA, and reproduced disease symptoms by introducing nematodes into beech buds.
identification: The nematode itself is too small for ordinary field identification. Dark bands between leaf veins are a useful warning sign, but laboratory examination confirms the organism.
actions: Seek a plant diagnostic service for suspicious beech leaves. Keep the tree's location and photographs with the report and avoid moving affected planting material.

Supported form is Litylenchus crenatae subsp. mccannii; the paper title sometimes omits the rank. UMD draws causality from Carta et al.; its regional symptom observations are independently authored. No origin or universal invasive-status claim made.

proposedDescription: Beefsteakplant is an aromatic annual in the mint family, native to Asia and introduced in many parts of North America. It has opposite, toothed leaves on square stems, with small flowers grouped along upright spikes. Common ornamental forms have broad, crinkled, purple to reddish leaves. Plants produce abundant seed and may appear beyond gardens along roadsides or in other disturbed ground. Despite its history of cultivation, it can be troublesome in pastures because the plant is toxic to livestock.
identification: Check for opposite, broad toothed leaves, square stems and small flowers in narrow spikes. Leaf color varies among forms and is not enough for identification.
actions: Keep suspected plants out of livestock forage and seek local Extension advice on pasture infestations. Where removal is appropriate, act before seed develops.
researchNotes: Species includes multiple varieties and cultivated forms; purple foliage is not universal. NC State provides independently authored horticultural and regional weed information; Kew/WCVP supports accepted name and range. No edible-use recommendation or nationwide invasive designation.

proposedDescription: Beet armyworm is a moth whose caterpillars feed on many vegetables, field crops and weeds. Young larvae gather together and scrape leaf surfaces, sometimes leaving thin, windowlike patches and loose webbing. Older caterpillars spread out, chew irregular holes and may enter developing fruit. They are usually green with lengthwise stripes and a small dark spot near the second pair of true legs. Adults are mottled gray-brown moths, while eggs occur in clusters beneath a covering of pale, hairlike scales.
identification: Look for smooth, striped caterpillars with a dark spot above the second true leg, scale-covered egg clusters and grouped young larvae. Similar armyworms require closer comparison.
actions: Inspect leaves and developing fruit regularly and preserve beneficial insects where possible. Have damaging caterpillars identified before choosing crop-specific controls.

proposedDescription: Bell's honeysuckle is a dense, many-stemmed shrub produced by crosses between Morrow's and Tatarian honeysuckles. It bears opposite, oval leaves and paired tubular flowers, often pink when fresh and yellow as they age. Red or orange berries follow and can be carried by birds. The hybrid is variable, with leaves and twigs ranging from nearly hairless to lightly downy. In parts of the northeastern and midwestern United States it grows along woodland edges, roadsides and old fields, sometimes forming dense stands.

proposedDescription: Polygonum patulum is a slender annual knotweed with upright stems that branch near the base. Native across parts of Europe and Asia, it occurs in fields, gardens and other open ground, including seasonally flooded places.

proposedDescription: Bengal trumpet is a long-lived climbing vine with large, pale blue to violet flowers and pale throats. Its opposite leaves are variable, often bearing broad teeth or shallow pointed lobes, and young stems are square in cross-section. Thickened underground roots help the plant persist. Native to southern Asia and grown for its flowers, it can become an environmental weed in warm regions such as Queensland. The blossoms attract bees, including large carpenter bees, and flowers may be followed by distinctly beaked capsules.

proposedDescription: Bent-grass nematode is a microscopic roundworm that develops inside abnormal growths in grass flower heads. These elongated galls replace developing seeds and can be concealed by the surrounding flower parts. Bentgrasses are the best-known hosts, and a modern study also confirmed the species in fowl bluegrass beside a Wyoming river. Older accounts assigned many other grasses to this nematode, but some of those records belong to different species. Accurate identification therefore depends on examining the nematodes, not just noticing damaged seed heads.
identification: Unusually elongated flower parts and seed-replacing galls are useful warning signs. Microscopic and, where needed, DNA examination are necessary for species identification.
actions: Do not distribute suspect grass seed lots. Ask a seed-testing or plant diagnostic laboratory to examine galls and advise on cleaning or disposal.
researchNotes: Strong taxonomy caveat: older A. agrostis sensu lato host and bacterial-toxicity accounts cannot be transferred indiscriminately. Roubtsova/Subbotin 2020 molecularly confirmed Poa palustris; Eisenback/Roane 2006 is an independent morphology-based grass-gall study, but its A. stolonifera host record predates the narrow modern synthesis. Nemaplex repeats both lineages and is not a third independent experiment. No chemical, hot-water or burning prescription.

proposedDescription: Agrostis castellana is a perennial bentgrass with fine, gray-green leaves and upright flowering stems. It forms tufts linked by slender underground stems, while its flower head spreads into a delicate branching shape and often narrows as it ages. The tiny flower clusters may be greenish or purple, with some bearing slender awns and others lacking them. Native around the Mediterranean and nearby Atlantic islands, it has been introduced elsewhere, including New Zealand, where it is known as dryland browntop.
identification: Look for fine gray-green leaves, underground spreading stems and an open flower head with a mixture of awned and awnless flower clusters. A grass key is needed.
actions: Have flowering material identified before managing an unfamiliar patch. Check local guidance and avoid moving seed or soil from unwanted stands.
researchNotes: Catalog Bentgrass is nonspecific; dryland browntop is supported by Edgar and Connor. Independent New Zealand flora and Kew/WCVP support morphology and range. No US invasive status inferred and no traits copied from unrelated Agrostis entries or old synonym descriptions.

proposedDescription: Lachnagrostis filiformis is a fine-leaved grass native to Australia, often growing on poorly drained or seasonally wet ground. Its loose, airy flower head branches widely above a tuft of narrow leaves, and the small green or purplish flower clusters carry bent bristles. At maturity, the stem commonly breaks beneath the flower head, allowing it to move away from the parent plant. Plants may behave as annuals or persist longer, and closely related grasses can be difficult to separate.
identification: Look for an open, often drooping flower head, narrow leaves and tiny bent awns. Mature heads may break away; a botanical key is needed for close relatives.
actions: Photograph mature flower heads and basal growth for identification. Check regional status before removal, since this grass is native in parts of its range.
researchNotes: Catalog common name Bentgrass is broad. VicFlora describes variation and difficult separation from L. aemula; no simple field cue is claimed diagnostic. Walsh/Stajsic's Victorian flora and Spooner's Western Australian account are independently authored; no US invasive status inferred.

proposedDescription: Bermuda buttercup is a bulb-forming perennial from southern Africa, with bright yellow flowers held above a loose cluster of leaves. Each leaf has three heart-shaped leaflets, often dotted with purple. Despite its common name, it is a wood sorrel rather than a true buttercup. In California it grows during the cooler, wetter part of the year and retreats to underground bulbs as weather warms. Those bulbs allow patches to return and can spread the plant when contaminated soil is moved.
identification: Look for three heart-shaped leaflets, clustered yellow flowers on leafless stalks and small underground bulbs. Distinguish it from low, creeping wood sorrels.
actions: Avoid moving soil from infested patches. Where removal is appropriate, collect bulbs carefully and revisit the area, since cutting off leaves alone leaves bulbs alive.
researchNotes: UC's California biology is kept regional; the same article includes O. corniculata, whose seed-based spread and management were not transferred. Kew-hosted Flora of Iraq is independently authored and supports bulb reproduction and southern African range. No claim that the species never produces viable seed worldwide.

proposedDescription: Bermudagrass is a low, wiry perennial grass that grows most actively in warm weather. It spreads through runners above ground and underground stems, both able to root and form new plants. Narrow leaves and fingerlike branches radiating from the tip of each flower stalk help distinguish a flowering patch. It is widely grown as turf, yet the same spreading growth makes it a persistent weed in gardens and planting beds. In cooler conditions the foliage turns brown as the grass becomes dormant.
identification: Check for rooting runners, underground stems, a fringe of white hairs where leaf meets sheath and three to seven fingerlike flower-head branches.
actions: Keep runners and contaminated soil out of beds where it is unwanted. Remove spreading stems repeatedly and monitor regrowth; fragments left in moist soil can root.
researchNotes: Species-specific UC IPM account and Utah State pest guide were read; no genus-level hybrid-turf facts used. Utah phenology is regional, so exact dormant months omitted. UC and USU are independently authored institutional guidance, with USU's own photographed specimens.

proposedDescription: Bhutan pine is an evergreen mountain tree from the Himalayan region, also known as Himalayan pine. Its long, gray-green needles grow in bundles of five and hang downward on older shoots, giving the branches a soft, drooping appearance. Long, resinous cones hang from stalks, while bark changes from smooth gray-green on young wood to darker, fissured scales with age. The species is grown as an ornamental beyond its native range and generally favors sunny sites with well-drained soil.
identification: Count five needles per bundle and look for long, drooping needles and long-stalked, resinous cones. Compare mature cones with other five-needle pines.
actions: Document needles, cones and overall form to confirm identification. Assess local planting or naturalization status before deciding whether any management is needed.
researchNotes: Oregon State horticultural observations and Kew/WCVP are independent sources. Common name Bhutan pine refers here to P. wallichiana; no claim about P. bhutanica. Ornamental cultivation does not establish invasive behavior, and variable hardiness and garden height estimates were omitted.

proposedDescription: Bicolored trailing ants are tiny, shiny ants with a dark head and abdomen contrasting with a much lighter middle section. Workers are less than two millimeters long and often forage on trees, shrubs and around buildings in warm climates. Colonies occupy small cavities, including spaces in twigs and bark, and may contain several queens. The ants take insects and sweet foods, including honeydew from plant-feeding bugs. Their small nests can travel with nursery plants and other material moved by people.
identification: Use magnification to check the dark head and abdomen, pale middle and two-part waist. Confirm a collected specimen because other small household ants can look similar.
actions: Inspect nursery plants and small cavities before moving them. Indoors, remove accessible food and seek species identification before selecting a targeted control.
researchNotes: Longino's original Costa Rican nest observations are independent of MacGown and Hill's 2010 Mississippi specimen report. The latter's nursery collection suggested transport but did not prove established Mississippi colonies; this distinction is retained. Old US range statements are not treated as current limits.

proposedDescription: Mouse-ear chickweed is a low, spreading perennial with small paired leaves and white flowers. Its softly hairy growth can blend into lawns until the flowers appear, each with five notched petals. Originally from Europe, it now grows widely in North America in fields, roadsides and other open, disturbed places. The flowers are small, with petals about as long as the green sepals beneath them. Those details help separate it from similar chickweeds.
identification: Look for opposite, untoothed leaves and small white flowers; compare petal length with the sepals before identifying it.
actions: Photograph the flowers, leaves and whole plant before seeking identification help. A record alone does not establish that removal is needed.
researchNotes: Go Botany explicitly treats subsp. vulgare; independently checked Flora Helvetica morphology. Avoided a blanket ecological-impact claim. Action is identification guidance.

proposedDescription: Large quaking grass has flower clusters that hang like little paper lanterns from fine stalks. The overlapping scales can turn brown or purple, and the loose clusters give this annual grass its distinctive nodding look. Native to the Mediterranean region, it grows in disturbed ground and has become established beyond its original range. Narrow, flat leaves form loose tufts beneath the flower stems. Its conspicuous clusters make it easier to recognize than many grasses.
identification: Look for relatively large, drooping oval flower clusters on threadlike stalks, with broad overlapping scales.
actions: Record a clear image of the flower clusters and leaf bases. Check local weed guidance before planting or moving seed.
researchNotes: Independent NSW and New Zealand floras corroborate morphology. Neither used to infer nationwide US invasive status; action is conservative prevention.

proposedDescription: Big trefoil is a perennial member of the pea family, with yellow flowers gathered in clusters above its leaves. Each leaf has five leaflets, though the lower pair sits close to the stem and can be easy to overlook. Hollow stems and creeping shoots help distinguish its growth. Native to Eurasia and North Africa, it has become established elsewhere, including moist disturbed ground in southwestern British Columbia. You may also find it listed as Lotus pedunculatus.
identification: Look for five leaflets, hollow stems and clusters of yellow pea-shaped flowers on long stalks.
actions: Take photographs of a complete leaf and flower cluster to distinguish it from other trefoils. Avoid moving unwanted plants or seed into natural areas.
researchNotes: Both independent floras explicitly link L. uliginosus and L. pedunculatus. Habitat and introduced-range example restricted to BC; no US impact inferred. Containment advice is precautionary.

proposedDescription: Bighead carp are large freshwater fish with oversized heads, low-set eyes and irregular dark blotches along their bodies. Rather than hunting larger prey, they strain tiny organisms and other food from the water. Introduced from Asia for pond management, they escaped into rivers and now occur in parts of the Mississippi River system. Their appetite for plankton can put them in competition with native fish, including paddlefish and young fish that depend on the same food.
identification: The eyes sit low on a very large head. Dark body blotches and a belly ridge extending only from the vent to the pelvic fins help distinguish it from silver carp.
actions: Do not move live fish between waters. Photograph a suspected catch and contact your state fisheries agency for identification and handling instructions.
researchNotes: Independent state agency syntheses corroborate identity, feeding and introduction; no unverified local occurrence or nationwide fishing rule. California handling rule not generalized.

proposedDescription: Bighead knapweed is a sturdy perennial topped with large, bright yellow flower heads. Beneath each head, overlapping brown, papery scales form a rounded cup. Once grown as a garden ornamental, it has escaped cultivation in parts of Washington, where it can compete with grasses. Its rough, pointed leaves become smaller farther up the stems. The showy flowers are followed by seeds that help it spread, making an escaped patch worth identifying before those heads mature.
identification: Look for yellow globe-shaped flower heads, brown overlapping bracts and rough lance-shaped leaves on upright stems.
actions: Where it is invasive, avoid planting it and prevent seed production. Ask your local weed program about removal; small plants may be dug out.
researchNotes: County weed-board field observations and independently authored botanical treatment hosted by Burke support description. Historical county locations not presented as a current complete distribution.

proposedDescription: Bigheaded ants get their name from the unusually large heads of their larger workers, which forage alongside many smaller ants. These small brown ants nest in soil, lawns and sheltered spaces beneath paving or pots, often leaving loose piles of sand. They feed on insects and sweet liquids such as honeydew. Established in many warm regions, including Florida, their large colonies can displace other ants and become a persistent household nuisance. Related native ants make careful identification important.
identification: Look for two distinct worker sizes, with conspicuously large heads on the larger workers. Have an expert confirm the species.
actions: Seek identification before treating. For an established infestation, coordinate with neighboring properties and use locally approved bait or professional guidance.
researchNotes: Independent UF field/extension account and Western Australian agency guide read. Avoided exporting Australian pesticide registrations or conflating paving disturbance with damage to building timber.

proposedDescription: Broadleaf bristlegrass is a tall, clump-forming perennial whose broad, pleated leaves can look quite different from ordinary lawn grasses. Its flowering stems carry long, branching clusters with fine bristles beside the small spikelets. It favors moist, sheltered places, including forest edges and stream margins, and has become established in Florida. Large rootstocks help the plant persist between growing seasons. A close look at the leaves and flower clusters is useful when separating it from other broad-leaved grasses.
identification: Look for broad, pleated leaf blades and long, branched flower clusters with bristles beneath individual spikelets.
actions: Photograph both the leaves and flowering stems. Seek local identification advice before moving or planting clumps near natural areas.

proposedDescription: Bigleaf periwinkle is an evergreen groundcover with trailing stems, broad paired leaves and blue-violet flowers. Planted in gardens for its dense cover, it can spread beyond beds when stems take root wherever they touch moist ground. Broken pieces can also travel in dumped garden waste or flowing water. Along shaded creeks and woodland edges in places such as California, established patches can crowd out native plants. Its larger, often heart-based leaves help distinguish it from small periwinkle.
identification: Check for opposite leaves with tiny hairs along their margins and five-lobed blue-violet flowers; small periwinkle has smaller, usually hairless-edged leaves.
actions: For small patches, remove rooted stems and underground parts, then revisit for regrowth. Keep fragments out of waterways and garden-waste dumps.
researchNotes: Regional impacts explicitly limited to documented settings. NC State horticultural account and Drewitz's California synthesis independently read.

proposedDescription: Birch leafminer is a small sawfly whose young feed between the upper and lower surfaces of birch leaves. Their feeding creates pale blotches that later turn brown, sometimes making a tree look badly scorched. Adults resemble tiny dark flies rather than wasps. Introduced to North America from the Old World, this species is one of several insects that mine birch leaves. Healthy, established trees often tolerate the damage, so brown foliage alone does not mean a tree is dying.
identification: Look for blotch-like mines with pale larvae inside fresh birch leaves. Several other birch leafminers cause similar damage, so species confirmation may need expert help.
actions: Check new leaves rather than treating old, empty mines. If damage is extensive or the tree is stressed, ask an extension office or qualified arborist to assess it.
researchNotes: University of Minnesota uses the older name Fenusa pusilla; Kirichenko et al. explicitly connect that name to F. pumila. Avoided conflating it with Profenusa thomsoni.

proposedDescription: Bird vetch is a climbing perennial with rows of small leaflets, curling tendrils and clusters of purple flowers gathered along one side of a stalk. It grows through meadows, roadsides and other open or disturbed places, using neighboring plants for support. Underground stems and seeds both help it spread. In Alaska, researchers have observed dense growth overtopping herbs and climbing shrubs at forest edges. Those tangled patches can change the space available to the vegetation beneath them.
identification: Look for compound leaves ending in branched tendrils and one-sided clusters of blue-purple pea flowers.
actions: Record the patch and photograph flowers and leaves. Avoid moving soil or seed-bearing vines from infested ground; seek local guidance for established patches.
researchNotes: Go Botany supplies independent morphology; Alaska assessment includes Lapina and Carlson's direct observations. Kept impact geography explicit and omitted speculative pollination effects.

proposedDescription: Birdsfoot trefoil is a low perennial with clusters of yellow pea-shaped flowers and slender seedpods that spread out like a bird's toes. Introduced as forage and for erosion control, it now grows along roadsides and in open grasslands. Its branching stems may lie close to the ground or rise above surrounding vegetation. proposedDescription: Spreading pearlwort is a tiny perennial that forms low patches of slender stems and narrow leaves. It often grows in moist ground, lawns and cracks in paving, where its size makes it easy to overlook. The flowers are very small, with white petals that may be shorter than the surrounding green sepals or absent altogether. Some stems root where they touch the ground. This plant is native in parts of North America but introduced elsewhere, so its local status matters when interpreting a record.

actions: Confirm both identity and local native status before removing it. Avoid carrying soil and plant fragments into sensitive habitats.

proposedDescription: Goutweed is a spreading perennial often planted as a leafy groundcover, including forms with creamy white leaf edges. Beneath the surface, branching rhizomes help it form dense patches that can be difficult to contain. Its leaves are divided into toothed leaflets, and small white flowers gather in broad, flat clusters above them. Originally from Europe and Asia, it has escaped gardens into shaded edges and woodlands. Dense growth can displace native herbs and leave less room for young trees to establish.

actions: Dig small patches carefully, removing rhizomes and revisiting for regrowth. Contain discarded plant material so living fragments do not establish elsewhere.

proposedDescription: Shampoo ginger is a tropical perennial with upright leafy stems and cone-shaped flower heads on separate, shorter stalks. The overlapping bracts begin green and become red as they mature, with small pale flowers emerging between them. It spreads from creeping rhizomes and favors moist, sheltered places. Known as awapuhi in Hawai‘i, it was brought there by early Polynesian voyagers and has a long cultural history. Its leafy growth can die back seasonally, while the underground stems remain ready to grow again.

proposedDescription: Black bamboo is a tall evergreen grass best known for canes that emerge green and darken as they mature. Narrow leaves form light, arching sprays above the distinctive stems. proposedDescription: Black bean bug is a small, shiny black insect that often gathers with others on plant stems and leaf stalks. proposedDescription: Black carp is a large, dark fish with broad scales and powerful teeth deep in its throat that can crush snails and mussels.
